{"type": "user", "message": {"role": "user", "content": [{"tool_use_id": "toolu_01WjbjjrssnbncM4QxL1nPJD", "type": "tool_result", "content": "# sideeye [![CI](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/actions/workflows/ci.yml?query=branch%3Amain) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/yottayoshida/sideeye)](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases/latest)

Sideeye finds out what your program leaves on disk when it dies at the worst possible moment. Declare an invariant — *"if this operation said it succeeded, this must still hold after a restart"* — and Sideeye kills your process before each state-changing operation, one crash world each, and brings back the earliest failing one as a replayable case. `sideeye demo`, trimmed, checked line by line in CI: ``` FAIL 1 of 6 explored worlds violated an invariant invariant built-in atomicity, and the checker earliest crash point 5 of 5 after unlink(…/state/key.json) before rename(…/state/key.json.tmp) path key.json observed present before and after the operation, but gone from the crashed state explored 6 worlds (crash points 5 + 1 baseline) checker falsified before the run (corrupted state -> check failed); ran in 6 world(s) case …/work/cases/000001.json not tested power loss, torn writes, concurrent processes ``` Counterexamples found: RuboCop, ImageMagick, the AWS CLI, [more](docs/found.md) — [four fixes](docs/case-studies.md). A target Sideeye cannot fully observe is UNKNOWN, never a silent PASS — except unrecorded writes under a directory a recorded `rename` moved in from outside, counted as `paths_attributed_to_rename` in every JSON report ([why](DESIGN.md#the-one-named-exception-a-directory-renamed-in-from-outside)). ## Installation Runs on macOS 14+ (Apple silicon) and Linux glibc (x86_64, aarch64): Homebrew, or a [release](https://github.com/yottayoshida/sideeye/releases) tarball run where you unpack it. Other platforms, building from source: [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md#platforms). ``` $ brew install yottayoshida/tap/sideeye $ tar xzf sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos.tar.gz && cd sideeye-v1.13.0-aarch64-macos $ ./sideeye version ``` ## Usage ``` $ sideeye demo $ sideeye preflight --state --operation "" $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --oracle /usr/bin/strace $ sideeye explore --config sideeye.toml --allow-unverified ``` - **`demo`** — sixty seconds, no compiler; one directory left under `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp`) with the saved case. Exit 1, the bug found, is success. - **`preflight`** — can Sideeye watch your tool? One observed run: `recording accepted`, or a refusal naming the detector. - **`explore`** — the real thing; the define in one file: ```toml [world] state = "./state" # your tool's state [define] cwd = "." # relative arguments resolve here setup = "mytool init" operation = "mytool rotate-key" # the shim is inserted into this one, not into setup or check check = "./check.sh" # exit 0 = invariant holds ``` `operation` is the one command the shim is inserted into; command strings split on spaces, no quoting. `--oracle` is a second witness, the kernel's account (Linux; on macOS, `--oracle-fs-usage`); without one, PASS needs `--allow-unverified`, and the report says so. `--shim` names the shim when it is not beside the binary; `--work` moves the scratch directory. Exit codes: **0 PASS, 1 FAIL, 2 UNKNOWN, 3 SETUP ERROR**. A FAIL saves a replayable case, and `sideeye evidence ` renders it for an issue tracker. Run `explore --config` in CI ([docs/ci-quickstart.md](docs/ci-quickstart.md)). For agents there is `sideeye mcp`, and three skills (`npx skills@1.7.1 add yottayoshida/sideeye`): [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md). ## Writing the check The check, like the setup, receives the state directory in `$SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR`. This one cross-examines the tool's own diagnostic; the violation is the claim and the observable truth disagreeing: ```sh claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null) || claim="unhealthy" "$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1 && reality="loadable" || reality="unloadable" case "$claim:$reality" in healthy:loadable | unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;; *) echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2; exit 1 ;; esac ``` Sideeye refuses to trust a checker it has not seen fail: it corrupts the state first. A checker that cannot fail makes the run UNKNOWN, not PASS; so does an exploration in which no world could have failed ([conditions](docs/report-schema.md)). ## What the target has to be Sideeye refuses to guess: outside these limits the verdict is UNKNOWN, naming the detector. Reasons: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#known-constraints-declared-not-hidden). - **Dynamically linked**, reaching files through libc; static only under `--observe supervised` (Linux). Hardened runtimes are refused. Threads are judged where a creation or a join the shim saw orders their writes. - **Under `--observe syscalls`, a process whose `SIGSYS` is blocked or reset dies at its first state-changing call** — an `exec`'d image the shim cannot reach, a `posix_spawn` child. - **Byte-repeatable writes** (`preflight --twice` checks), **state in one directory**, **a clean run exits its declared success status**. - **Other processes take turns with the state**, and every writing child is reaped; a process boundary needs Linux's `--oracle`, and one that leaves its process group is judged only where the engine can hold the run in a cgroup (Linux) — otherwise UNKNOWN. - **On macOS, a framework Python's `bin/python3` is a launcher**; Sideeye refuses it and names the interpreter to run instead. No language model decides a verdict; a PASS is a search record naming what was *not* tested. ## Documentation [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md) · [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md) · [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) · [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) · [docs/report-schema.md](docs/report-schema.md) · [docs/target-classes.md](docs/target-classes.md) · [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) · [docs/](docs/) ## License [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE), at your option. # Apparatus: declaring what a deterministic run depends on A target that stamps the clock, draws random ids or numbers its files from an inode is refused at the baseline (`baseline_violates_invariant`, naming the path — see "Byte-repeatable writes" in the README's limits). The cohorts that measured such targets got past the wall by pinning the source of variation outside the target: a faked clock, a seeded `os.urandom`, a stand-in compiler. Every one of those lived in a launcher script or in `setup`, and the committed define said nothing about it. `[define] apparatus` is where the define says it (ADR 0041). Sideeye applies none of it. After `setup` and before the first snapshot it checks that every entry it can check is present in the environment the operation will inherit, and refuses the run as SETUP ERROR — naming the entry and what it looked at — when one is not. The report carries the list as declared in `apparatus`, and the entries it could not check in `apparatus_unchecked`. ```toml [define] setup = "./pins/setup.sh" # generates sitecustomize.py, plants the flag file operation = "borg create ::a /src" apparatus = [ "env:FAKETIME=@2024-01-01 00:00:00", "preload:libfaketime", "pythonpath:sitecustomize.py", "note:borg's --no-cache-sync is passed on the command line", ] ``` (The example spans lines for reading; the accepted form is one `[` ... `]` line, the same as the commands' argv form.) | entry | what is checked | where the device is set | |---|---|---| | `env:NAME` | `NAME` is set in the environment the operation inherits | the launcher, or the shell | | `env:NAME=VALUE` | set, and equal to `VALUE` — for devices whose value *is* the device (`PAPIS_NP=0`, `FAKETIME=...`) | same | | `preload:LIB` | a line of `/etc/ld.so.preload` names a library whose basename starts with `LIB` | the launcher writes the line (needs root). Linux only | | `pythonpath:FILE` | some entry of `PYTHONPATH` has `FILE` directly under it. Existence only: the content is not judged | `setup` generates the file; the launcher exports `PYTHONPATH` | | `note:TEXT` | nothing — carried, listed as unchecked | wherever it lives (an hgrc line, a container's seccomp profile, a pin applied inside the operation's own command line) | ## The one thing to know about `preload:` **Never through `LD_PRELOAD`.** Sideeye replaces `LD_PRELOAD` with its own shim for every child it spawns (that is how it records the operation), so a library the launcher put there does not reach the operation — and it would be a silent absence: the run records, the clock is real, the baseline refuses without saying why. If `LD_PRELOAD` does name the library and `/etc/ld.so.preload` does not, the refusal says exactly that. `/etc/ld.so.preload` is global. A library named there rides on **every** process on the machine for the duration, the engine's own `/bin/sh -c` included (the shape that once made every world report `child_process_detected`) and, under `--oracle`, on `strace`'s children. The cohorts did this inside a container, and that is the recipe: pin in a container, name the pin in the define. A pid pin has the same global reach and no per-target form Sideeye can see, which is why cohort 4's `pin-getpid.c` was applied inside the operation's command line and is declared as a `note:`. On macOS there is no global preload file and Sideeye owns `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`; a define with a `preload:` entry is refused there as unsatisfiable. ## What the check does not prove - `pythonpath:` proves the file exists under some entry, not that it is the file the define meant, nor that Python will import it first. - `env:NAME` without a value proves presence, not that the value is the one the run needs; write the value when the value is the device. - The checker's environment is the define's business. A checker may drop a device on purpose (cohort 3's cargo-r2 unsets `RUSTC` to compare against the real compiler); the check is about the operation's environment only. - The saved case does not carry the declaration. A replay without the apparatus is not silent — the baseline does not repeat the recorded bytes and the refusal names the path — but the case file itself does not say which device was missing. ## Reading a byte difference A byte-layer `baseline_violates_invariant` says where the two runs' bytes first differ, how long the differing stretch is in each run and what kind of bytes it holds; `preflight --twice` says the same and quotes both stretches (#688, [docs/cli.md](cli.md#usage)). Neither says what produced the difference — ten decimal digits are a clock in one tool and a counter in the next — so the table is where to start looking, not a diagnosis. The devices it names are the ones the cohorts used (below). | what the stretch holds | what to check first | how the define says it | |---|---|---| | decimal digits, the same length in both runs | whether the tool writes the time, a counter, or its process id | a pinned clock (`preload:libfaketime` with `env:FAKETIME=...`), or the tool's own switch for it, in `apparatus` | | hex digits | whether it is an id or a hash the tool draws fresh each run | a seeded or pinned source (`pythonpath:sitecustomize.py` pinning `os.urandom`) in `apparatus` | | any kind, in a file nothing reads back as state — a cache, a log, an editor's message file | whether anything the operation's user depends on reads that file | `scratch` for the path; the report then names it in `not tested` | | bytes outside printable text, inside a compressed or binary format | whether the format carries a time stamp or an id of its own (PNG text chunks, archive headers) | the tool's option that leaves it out, if it has one, on the operation's command line, and a `note:` saying so | A stretch the table does not cover is still an observation about the target: the run is refused because a second clean run does not leave what the first one did, which is the README's byte-repeatable-writes limit, and no declaration makes two different results the same one. ## A tool's own switch for one thread A run whose judged directory is written by two threads of one process, with nothing recorded ordering their writes, is refused `multiple_threads_detected` (the README's threads limit), and the refusal's next step sends the reader here. Many runtimes put file calls on a pool of threads, and many have a switch that makes the pool one thread. Set the switch in the environment Sideeye runs in — Sideeye applies none of it — and declare it, so the report says what the run ran under and a run without it stops as a SETUP ERROR rather than being judged as something else. Over MCP the server passes its children `PATH` and only the names `SIDEEYE_MCP_CHILD_ENV` lists (`docs/mcp.md`): list the switch there too, or the declared run stops as that SETUP ERROR. A verdict under the switch is a verdict about the tool run that way. A race two threads produce is not in it; what the switch takes away is that the trace's numbering would name a different operation on the next run. | switch | how the define says it | moved past the wall | not moved, and why | record | |---|---|---|---|---| | Node: `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1` | `env:UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1` | ten of the thirteen Node targets that met the wall on v1.10.0 — joplin and stylelint to PASS; prettier, svgo, `npm pkg set`, eslint, dotenvx, bibtex-tidy and glTF-Transform to FAIL; lingui to its next wall — and yarn, trash-cli, cspell and capacitor (the last two on Node 22). Without it, all thirteen refuse | Bitwarden CLI (its lock directory is taken on the pool thread), vercel (`mkdirp` of its state directory on the pool thread at every start), gemini-cli (the pool thread writes its home registry) | `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-3/`, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-4/`, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-10-uv-threadpool/` | | Go: `GOMAXPROCS=1` | `env:GOMAXPROCS=1` | doctl, infracost and plakar, under `--observe supervised` | OpenTofu: with one P the writing thread is still the scheduler's choice per run | `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-3/`, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-4/` | | zstd: `--single-thread --no-asyncio` | on the operation's command line, and a `note:` | zstd 1.5.7 `--rm` (`--single-thread` alone still writes through an I/O thread) | — | `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-3/` | | beets: `threaded: no` | a line in its configuration, and a `note:` | beets 2.1.0 `import` | — | `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-3/` | | Rust: `RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1 TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS=1` | — | none: measured, and none of four moved | a second writer neither variable removes — rustic's one rayon worker deletes the old snapshot while the main thread writes the index; prek and steamguard-cli write from two threads of their own; codex's start-up threads make and clear `tmp/arg0` beside the thread writing `config.toml` | `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-3/`, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-4/` | | lz4: `-T1` | — | none: measured, and it did not move | lz4 1.10.0: an I/O thread writes the blocks, and `-T#` is its only thread switch | `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-3/`, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-09-followups-4/` | Under `--observe supervised` no join is recorded, nor which thread a creation made, so a switch is the only way past there: recording creations and exits from outside was measured and not built (#687, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-10-thread-order/`). ## A checker is the declared invariant's sharp end: a command Sideeye runs over each crashed state, exit 0 meaning the invariant holds. It is the layer that found the timewarrior bug, and the layer easiest to get quietly wrong. Everything below is a real committed checker, or a failure pattern with the run that taught it — nothing was invented for this page.

Before any exploration, Sideeye **falsifies** the checker: it corrupts a copy of the state on purpose and requires the checker to go red. A checker that cannot fail anything is refused (`checker_not_falsified`), never trusted. Then it shows the checker the state the define starts from — restored the way every world starts from it, so what a restore does not carry ([docs/cli.md](cli.md)) is not there, whatever your setup left — and requires it to pass: a checker that rejects that state is refused too (`checker_rejects_initial_state`, #756), because the world killed before the first operation holds exactly that state, and nothing the target did is in it. A checker has to hold before the operation as well as after it — accept the old value and the new one, not only the one the operation writes. The recipes below are about the subtler failures that gate cannot catch.

A refusal that is not about the checker but about two clean runs leaving different bytes (`baseline_violates_invariant` on the byte layer) is read with [docs/apparatus.md](apparatus.md#reading-a-byte-difference), which maps what the difference looks like to `scratch` and `apparatus`.

A checker finds the state directory in `SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR`, the absolute path of the `state` you declared, resolved through any symlink — the setup, the operation and a recovery receive it too. Recipe 1's header also names `TOY_STATE`: the name the demo toy reads, which Sideeye sets to the same path for every command, so the checkers written against it keep working. A new checker reads `SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR`.

## Recipe 1 — cross-examine the tool's own diagnostic

`spike/check.sh`, the acceptance toy's checker (the README quotes part of it): run the tool's `doctor`, run the operation that depends on the same state, and require the two to **agree** — healthy things must work, unhealthy things must say so. A target is allowed to be broken as long as it says so; the violation is the *mismatch*, a diagnostic answering "healthy" over a store the tool itself cannot read.

#!/bin/sh
# The L2 checker: cross-examine the diagnostic command against reality.
#
# The invariant is not "the key is readable" — a target is allowed to be broken as
# long as it says so. The invariant is that `doctor`'s claim and the observable truth
# agree. Both directions are violations: claiming health while the key cannot be read,
# and claiming trouble while it can.
#
# Runs after a restart, in a fresh process, exactly as DESIGN §12 requires. Exit 0
# means the invariant holds.
#
# Environment:
#   TOY    path to the toy binary
#   TOY_STATE  state directory (passed through to the toy)

set -u

: "${TOY:?check.sh needs TOY to point at the binary under test}"

if claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null); then
    :
else
    claim="unhealthy"
fi

if "$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    reality="loadable"
else
    reality="unloadable"
fi

case "$claim:$reality" in
    healthy:loadable)     exit 0 ;;
    unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;;
    *)
        echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2
        exit 1
        ;;
esac
```

## Recipe 2 — the non-destruction form

`spike/loop-closure-timew/define/check.sh`, the checker behind the timewarrior finding — its one canonical text, beside `setup.sh` and `operation`; the scripts that stage or replay the define (`stage.sh`, `dogfood-timew-replay.sh`) copy the checker and setup and read the operation from there rather than carrying their own, and the frozen v0.4 recipe `spike/dogfood-timew.sh` keeps a copy the unknown-rate corpus pins, a record rather than a consumer (#65): after `timew undo`, the export must have removed *either nothing or exactly the newest interval*. The first draft demanded that undo always remove something — which condemns a correct recovery along with the bug, because a crash may have beaten the intent's commit; `spike/dogfood-timew.sh` carries that rationale beside the checker text. The admission is written down too: this form deliberately allows an undo that always no-ops, so the loop-closure apparatus scores a fix that *lobotomizes* the feature as a failure on a separate gate — declared before the run, not discovered after (`BUILDLOG.md`). One limit the code below makes visible and the sentence above does not: the comparison is over the *set* of interval keys, so it is blind to multiplicity — an undo that left a duplicate of an interval already present would add no new key and pass. The claim the checker actually carries is about which keys appear and disappear, not how many times each does.

To adapt this: Swap `timew export` / `timew undo` for your target's reader and recovery command, and the interval keying for whatever your reader's records are identified by.

#!/bin/sh
# The declared invariant (L2 checker), non-destruction form: undo must remove either
# nothing or exactly the interval timew's own export names as most recent — never an
# older committed interval, and it must not invent intervals. Removing nothing is
# allowed because a crash may have beaten the intent's commit.
#
# This file is the one canonical text of the checker (#65). The scripts that stage or
# replay the define copy it from here; none carries its own. The frozen v0.4 recipe,
# whose bytes the unknown-rate corpus pins, is a record rather than a consumer.
set -eu
before=$(timew export) || exit 1
timew undo >/dev/null || exit 1
after=$(timew export) || exit 1
BEFORE="$before" AFTER="$after" python3 - <<'PY'
import json, os, sys

def key(iv):
    return (iv["start"], iv.get("end", ""), ",".join(iv.get("tags", [])))

before = json.loads(os.environ["BEFORE"])
after = json.loads(os.environ["AFTER"])
if not before:
    print("export was empty before undo: the seeded interval is gone", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
newest = min(before, key=lambda iv: iv["id"])  # id 1 is timew's own "most recent"
b = sorted(key(iv) for iv in before)
a = sorted(key(iv) for iv in after)
added = [k for k in a if k not in b]
removed = [k for k in b if k not in a]
if added:
    print("undo added intervals:", added, file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
if removed not in ([], [key(newest)]):
    print("undo removed the wrong change: timew's own export named", key(newest),
          "as most recent, but undo removed", removed, file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
PY

- **Demanding destruction.** A checker that requires the operation to have visibly happened condemns correct crash recovery along with the bug (recipe 2). Allow the no-op; let a separate gate judge whether a fix gutted the feature.

# The L2 checker: cross-examine the diagnostic command against reality.
#
# The invariant is not "the key is readable" — a target is allowed to be broken as
# long as it says so. The invariant is that `doctor`'s claim and the observable truth
# agree. Both directions are violations: claiming health while the key cannot be read,
# and claiming trouble while it can.
#
# Runs after a restart, in a fresh process, exactly as DESIGN §12 requires. Exit 0
# means the invariant holds.
#
# Environment:
#   TOY    path to the toy binary
#   TOY_STATE  state directory (passed through to the toy)

set -u

: "${TOY:?check.sh needs TOY to point at the binary under test}"

if claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null); then
    :
else
    claim="unhealthy"
fi

if "$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    reality="loadable"
else
    reality="unloadable"
fi

case "$claim:$reality" in
    healthy:loadable)     exit 0 ;;
    unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;;
    *)
        echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2
        exit 1
        ;;
esac

# nothing or exactly the interval timew's own export names as most recent — never an
# older committed interval, and it must not invent intervals. Removing nothing is
# allowed because a crash may have beaten the intent's commit.

timew undo >/dev/null || exit 1
after=$(timew export) || exit 1

    return (iv["start"], iv.get("end", ""), ",".join(iv.get("tags", [])))

after = json.loads(os.environ["AFTER"])

a = sorted(key(iv) for iv in after)
added = [k for k in a if k not in b]

    print("undo added intervals:", added, file=sys.stderr)

`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/defines/useradd/check.sh`, the checker behind the 2026-10-14 mechanisms run's `useradd` FAIL (#861). `useradd` replaces `passwd`, `shadow`, `group` and `gshadow` one after another, each whole through a temporary and a rename, so a kill between two of them leaves every file intact and the four contradicting each other — and the built-in atomicity form, which judges each file on its own (`group` and `gshadow` old-or-new; `passwd` and `shadow` by their history form, which does not judge an appended tail), has nothing to say. ## Recipe 6 — the next run must still go through

`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/defines/alembic/check.sh`, the checker behind the same run's Alembic FAIL. With an `env.py` that does not apply the workaround SQLAlchemy's SQLite dialect documents, a batch migration on SQLite commits its temporary table alone — Python's `sqlite3` sends no `BEGIN` before DDL — and the copy, the drop, the rename and the version later. Killed between, nothing legs a, b and c read is wrong: the recorded revision, the table's shape and every row are whole (read after the recovery had been tried), and those legs passed in all 28 of the 43 explored worlds that FAILed; what is left besides is the temporary table, inferred from the two commits and seen in the state rebuilt by hand — the world's record lists no tables. Leg d, the recovery the user would run — the same `alembic upgrade head` — failed in all 28, and it was the only red leg in each. So the leg to copy is the next run's exit status, taken as part of the invariant rather than as a step before it. The database and its journal are declared `scratch` in `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/defines/alembic/sideeye.toml`: SQLite leaves them torn by design and repairs them on the next open (Recipe 4's contract), and without the declaration the built-in layer would judge those torn bytes itself — the reason the define gives, not something this run measured, since it declared them from the start.

Two things not to copy. Leg b picks the table shape it expects from leg a's input, the revisions recorded: when the version table holds none of the revisions the checker knows, b goes red with a. A version table naming a known revision beside another fails a — and d, since Alembic cannot upgrade from it — but not b: that is what the control for leg a built (`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/transcripts/controls.txt`), so the coupling shows only in the case the controls did not build. The same run's Django checker had the same coupling and was fixed by counting only the migrations it knows (`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/SELECTION.md`, "Checker controls"). And the recovery's output is cut to its last line (`tail -1`), which for SQLAlchemy is a link, so the world's record does not say which error the next run met. This one is shown as it ran, because the run's record is of these bytes.

    a = "ok" if vers in (["r1"], ["r2"]) else "FAIL(alembic_version %s)" % vers

## Failure patterns, each with the run that taught it

- **A broken state the recovery heals is no red.** A checker that runs the tool's recovery first has to be shown broken states the recovery cannot repair. In the 2026-10-14 mechanisms run, update-alternatives' first broken state for leg b pointed the link under its alternatives directory at the other editor; the checker's recovery, the same `--install`, put the link back, and the checker passed it — correctly — so the control said nothing about leg b until the broken state was one `--install` leaves alone (the generic link replaced by a plain file). The first form is recorded in prose, not in a transcript (`spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/SELECTION.md`, and the comment in `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/defines/alternatives/legs.sh`); the run's one-broken-state-per-leg controls are `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/apparatus/controls.sh`, with their output in `spike/dogfood/2026-10-14-mechanisms/transcripts/controls.txt`.
- **Exit-0-on-unreadable.** todoman's `list` prints a traceback and exits 0 — it answers "nothing wrong" precisely when it could not look. The falsification gate refused it: the first real checker rejected as unfalsifiable, as opposed to a synthetic `/bin/true` (`BUILDLOG.md`, the todoman entry). The committed fix is a strict wrapper — exit 0 AND no error text in the output (`spike/dogfood-todoman.sh`).
- **Demanding destruction.** A checker that requires the operation to have visibly happened condemns correct crash recovery along with the bug (recipe 2). Allow the no-op; let a separate gate judge whether a fix gutted the feature.
- **Counting lines when you mean occurrences.** `grep -c` counts lines; devtodo rewrites its whole store onto one XML line, so a duplicated note still counted as 1. `spike/assisted/devtodo/ops/check.sh` counts occurrences instead (`grep -o` piped to a line count) and records the review finding that caught it.
- **Asserting what you did not observe.** The general shape behind all of the above: the claim and the observable truth must agree. Every blind-campaign checker under `spike/blind-hunt/`, `spike/blind-hunt2/` and `spike/blind-hunt3/` ships with a red suite beside it proving each leg can individually fail — the cheapest way to know a checker is load-bearing.
- **A scratch file is not a counterexample — and only a checker knows which is which.** git commit reaches a full verdict and FAILs at one crash point: COMMIT_EDITMSG, opened with truncation before the message is written, torn to empty by a kill in that window. It is not a git bug — git rewrites the file on the next commit and never reads a torn one — and L0 has no way to know a file is scratch (DESIGN §12's per-file atomicity exempts no file *by its role* — a scratch file is judged like any other). The taught fix: a target with scratch files needs a checker carrying the *real* integrity claim — the same run with `git fsck --connectivity-only` as the checker accepted every crash world, because git's actual durability (objects, refs, index) held in all of them. An L0-only FAIL on a scratch path is the tool doing what it is defined to do, and the checker is where the definition gets sharper. Measured 2026-08-11, git 2.39.5, thirty-four worlds; the run and the ruling live in issue #35 and the freeze audit's row for it. **A second example, Borg (cohort 2, 2026-08-21), shows the same shape arriving a different way: the target creates the scratch path and the measurement setup relocates it into the judged root. The define's r2 repointed `BORG_BASE_DIR` because worlds refused otherwise, which brought Borg's own client cache inside the state root the engine rolls back, and all three L0 violations landed in that cache's in-place rewrite. The recipe held without change: the checker carried Borg's real integrity claim (stale-lock removal, `borg check`, base conservation, old-or-new listing) and the contract held in all 119 worlds. What that means for a `#!` script: the kernel hands execution to the interpreter, so the insertion has to reach *that* image rather than the file you named. Whether it can is a property of the interpreter and of the machine — a statically linked one takes no insertion anywhere, and on macOS a platform binary such as `/bin/sh` may have the variable stripped before it starts — so the same define can reach a verdict on one machine and refuse with `no_shim_marker` on another. Naming an executable image directly takes the question away.

A bare name is refused only when every file of that name on `PATH` fails this way, because execvp moves on to the next one. The setup is asked about before it runs, and that refusal leaves nothing on disk; the operation and the check after the setup has run, so a setup may build or write them — but a checker the operation itself would create is refused, so write it in `setup`. Under `--observe supervised` and `--oracle` the operation is launched from the first file of that name on `PATH` with no fallback, so a broken first file with a working one behind it passes the question and fails at the spawn. The `[recovery]` commands are not asked about — a recovery changes no verdict and no exit code, so one that cannot start shows as `recovery.result` `unknown` (#701, ADR 0092).

The quiet case is worse: a tool that walks up the tree to find its project, as git does, can find a *different* one above Sideeye's directory and succeed there, and nothing refuses. Every report produced after the `cwd` is resolved says which directory the commands ran in: `command_cwd` in the JSON and a `cwd` line in the text — on an UNKNOWN under `next`, in the verdict blocks, and in `preflight`'s report, whose `next` hint carries the `--cwd` it was given — with `(none declared: Sideeye's own)` when nothing was declared (#647). It sees nothing when the command finds a different file where it ran and succeeds, or writes outside the state directory through an argument that names nothing either side — which is why the README's toml example declares `cwd = "."`. (Left over from an earlier run it would resolve, which is worse — the define would work on one machine and not on a clean one.) Build such a directory before Sideeye starts — in CI, in the step before the one that runs it.

143	## What it is for after the first find
144	
145	The finding is not the durable artifact — the declaration is. A `sideeye.toml` and its checker are the question, not the answer, so re-asking it after the tool changes is `explore --config` again, and the report says what it looked at that time rather than assuming the last run still holds. A saved case is deliberately narrower: it names one crash point in one recording, and when the recording moves underneath it the answer is `case no longer applies` rather than a silent pass — which is what makes a case worth keeping in CI. This repository keeps its own oldest finding that way, re-recorded under the current trace contract on every push to main and every pull request (the `timew-regression` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`). And because a target Sideeye cannot fully observe is UNKNOWN and never exit 0, a machine caller can tell *checked and clean* from *not checked*, which is the distinction an unattended run has to get right. What none of that does is constrain what your declared operation may do — that boundary is the config you vet, as [the MCP page](mcp.md) says.

operation = "mytool rotate-key" # the shim is inserted into this one, not into setup or check

command   = "mytool repair"     # the string form only

What that means for a `#!` script: the kernel hands execution to the interpreter, so the insertion has to reach *that* image rather than the file you named. Whether it can is a property of the interpreter and of the machine — a statically linked one takes no insertion anywhere, and on macOS a platform binary such as `/bin/sh` may have the variable stripped before it starts — so the same define can reach a verdict on one machine and refuse with `no_shim_marker` on another. (Left over from an earlier run it would resolve, which is worse — the define would work on one machine and not on a clean one.) Build such a directory before Sideeye starts — in CI, in the step before the one that runs it.
- `apparatus` names the devices a deterministic run depends on — a faked clock, a pinned `os.urandom`, a stand-in compiler — so the define is the whole question and the report says what it ran under. Sideeye applies none of it; after `setup` it checks that each `env:`, `preload:` (a line of `/etc/ld.so.preload`) and `pythonpath:` entry is present in the environment the operation inherits and refuses the run as SETUP ERROR when one is not. `note:` entries are carried unchecked. Recipes and the one thing to know about global preloads: [docs/apparatus.md](apparatus.md).
- `scratch` names the paths under `state` that nobody depends on — git's `COMMIT_EDITMSG`, a tool's own cache — each entry covering the path itself and everything beneath it. The built-in invariants judge none of them, in no world: not their bytes, not their presence, whether the recording had them before, after, or both, so a torn scratch file no longer decides the verdict and a scratch file whose bytes differ between two clean runs no longer refuses the run. The price is paid in the open: the report carries the declaration verbatim, its `atomicity` line says how many recorded paths the declaration matched, `not tested` names it, and the saved case carries it (a define that declared everything reads `0 path(s) judged pre-or-post` — and, with no checker to judge the worlds instead (a marker has nothing to judge there either), is refused `nothing_could_fail`, because no world in it could have failed (ADR 0091)). What scratch does not silence: a state that changed with no operation recorded, a child the engine could not account for, an entry kind or a file size the snapshot refuses, a tree still being written when it is sampled twice — those are about what the engine observed, not about what is durable. And a checker is still the only thing that says the state is *correct*; scratch only stops the built-in layers from saying it is not (ADR 0043).
- `[recovery]` (or `--recovery` with `--recovery-check`) asks a second question about each FAIL: what does the tool's own recovery do to the state the crash left? **Declaring a recovery changes no verdict and no exit code; for each saved FAIL world it adds what the tool's own recovery did when handed that world's crash state — its names, kinds, contents and permission bits (a directory with its owner's bits added), not its timestamps, owners, or set-id and sticky bits.** After the exploration has decided its verdict, and only when there is a FAIL, the recovery checker is first shown a state whose every file holds distinct junk and must reject it, and then the completed, uncrashed state with `command` run on it, and must accept what that leaves; then, for the earliest exhibit and the checker exhibit (once if they are one world), the crash state is rebuilt in `state`, `command` runs, the state is sampled twice to see it has stopped changing, and `check` judges it. The report's `earliest.recovery` and `checker_earliest.recovery` say `pass`, `fail` or `unknown` with the time taken, the `recovery` line says what the result rests on, and the evidence bundle carries the result. `fail` means the recovery ran, ended and was rejected; a recovery that could not be started, exited 125, 126 or 127 (the codes the engine's own child uses before exec), overran `--world-timeout`, left something still writing or running where its cgroup could not stop it, or whose checker accepted the junk or rejected the completed state is `unknown`, never `fail`. Where the engine can make cgroups (Linux, as for a world), each recovery command and check runs in one of its own and everything it started is stopped when it exits — so a daemon the recovery starts does not reach the next leg, a check that needs that daemon running cannot be judged this way, and a recovery that hands the rest of its repair to a process it leaves is cut short there — the `recovery` line says how many processes each command left. Five limits come with it. The rebuilt state carries the crash's permission bits (since #678, ADR 0109) but restore-time timestamps and the engine's ownership, so a recovery that decides by modification time (make, ninja) sees every file as newly written — a `pass` from such a tool can be manufactured by that — and two names of one file come back as two files (ADR 0006). Only the saved exhibits are recovered, and the `recovery` line says how many of the run's failing worlds that was. The state directory afterwards holds what the last recovery left, not the baseline's result. Where the engine cannot make cgroups (macOS, or a Linux host without one to make), only the command's process group is stopped: a process that left the group, and anything a recovery writes outside the state directory anywhere, survives into the next leg — the next exhibit or the completed-state control — and can change what that leg reports. And the crash snapshots of the saved exhibits are held in memory until the exploration ends, so a run near the machine's memory can stop at a later world's snapshot where it would not have without a recovery. And a recovery that never ends holds the run the way a checker does unless `--world-timeout` bounds it. Both keys take the string form only: on a replay the same two commands travel as flags — accepted there, unlike the rest of the define, and printed on the replay line single-quoted — and a flag has no argv form (ADR 0072).
- Every define command — setup, operation, check, and a recovery's command and check — finds the state directory in `SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR`: the absolute path of `state`, resolved through any symlink, so a checker reads `"$SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR/…"` rather than a path relative to itself. `TOY_STATE`, the name the demo toy reads, carries the same path to every command, so a checker already written against it runs unchanged (#708).
- Every command Sideeye runs — your setup, operation and checker among them — starts with its standard input at end-of-file, on the CLI and MCP paths alike. A target that reads stdin sees EOF, never the terminal or pipe Sideeye itself was started from: that input is the caller's, not the define's, and a committed define has to mean the same run everywhere.
- `--shim` names the interposition library when it is not beside the binary (the tarball and zig-out layouts are found on their own). **A run that found its shim this way names none on its `replay` line or preflight's `next` line** (#827, ADR 0130), so a pasted line runs with the `sideeye` first on `PATH` and the shim found beside its real path, after an upgrade has removed the install it came from too — a `sideeye` that cannot find its own shim refuses, naming `--shim`, and a release whose trace contract changed answers `case_no_longer_applies` for an older case; a run given `--shim` names that path, as before. The `reproduce` line runs without Sideeye, so it names the shim's resolved path, and that path goes stale when an upgrade removes it. The search that finds it on its own **declines a candidate it cannot attribute** — a symlink, or a file owned by none of {you, root, the owner of the `sideeye` binary} — and says so rather than using it (#423, ADR 0044); a path you pass here is used as named and not checked. The check is a mitigation, not a boundary: it inspects a pathname, and the dynamic linker resolves that pathname again when the target starts. `--work` moves the scratch directory for traces and cases (default `/tmp/sideeye-work`). **It has to be yours** (#692, ADR 0099): the cases saved there are commands a replay runs, so a work directory Sideeye did not just create is refused before setup runs when its last component is a symlink (yours or not), when it is not a directory, when its name ends in `..`, when another user owns it — root included, unless you are root — or when its kind or owner cannot be read; the refusal names the directory and why, and Sideeye writes nothing under it (a `--json` report you point there is still written, as every refusal's is). A name that cannot be resolved at all is refused as before, naming the error. The way past is a name that does not exist yet, which Sideeye creates as yours, or a directory of your own. What used to run and now refuses: a link of your own at the name — pass the directory it points to — another user on the same host who made `/tmp/sideeye-work` first, `sudo sideeye` pointed at a directory you made, and a root container handed a bind mount your host user made. This too is a mitigation, not a boundary: it inspects the name once, and anyone who can write the directory's parent can swap it afterwards. **A symlink at the trace path is refused rather than followed — by every process the shim is loaded into when it writes the trace (#488), and by the engine when it reads that trace back (#489).** The engine removes the file before each run, but every process the shim reaches opens the name again afterwards and the later ones have nothing standing in front of them, so without the write-side refusal a link planted there would append the run's records to whatever it points at; without the read-side one, the account the verdict is drawn from would be whatever that link pointed at. A **FIFO** appearing at that path after the engine's own removal of it is refused on both sides as well: the read takes regular files only (#400), and the write does two things that answer different cases (#492): it opens **non-blocking**, so a FIFO with no reader fails outright instead of waiting for one — this is the half that stops the wait, in a constructor that runs before the target's `main`, inside a recording run with nothing to time it out — and it then asks what the descriptor turned out to be, closing it unless it is an ordinary file, which is the half that catches a FIFO somebody is already reading, along with a device or a socket. The one thing the write side leaves standing is a kind it could not read at all, a `statx` that fails: a host lacking it goes on refusing with `unresolvable_path`, which names a cause, rather than with a silence that names none. What is **not** refused: a **hard link** is the same file rather than a pointer to one, so no open flag sees it, on either side. Nor is the target on the other side of a boundary here — it holds the trace path in its own environment and can write the work directory, so a target that wants to hand Sideeye a trace it wrote itself is not something this or any flag stops.
- `--json <path>` writes the same report as JSON, for a machine to branch on. **What is at the path when the flag is read is removed only when it is a report Sideeye wrote — a file holding one JSON document, and nothing after it, whose `schema` is `sideeye/report` or `sideeye/preflight`, however it is formatted — or an empty file** (#818). Anything else there — a symbolic link, a directory, a FIFO, a device, the case or the config this same run reads, a log of reports one per line, any other file, or a name whose kind cannot be read — is refused as SETUP_ERROR `define_invalid`, the message naming the path and what it is, and left as it was; that refusal produces no document, so it writes no report, at that path or at an earlier `--json` in the same command, and no `json sha256=` line. The report itself goes through a temporary file this run creates new beside the path, then moves into place. The check reads the name once, when the flag is read: it stops a mistyped path, not a process that can write the directory, and whatever appears at the path during the run is replaced by the report as before. When the file is in place one line goes to stderr, in a single write: `sideeye: json sha256=<hex>;`, the digest of exactly the bytes written -- so a machine that receives the report through a directory the judged program can also write can tell the file it opens from one written after it. When the report could not be written the line reads `sideeye: json sha256=none;`. It is exactly one line per run that got as far as producing a document — a report, or `preflight`'s own (#717) — it is not part of the report schema, and a reader should count it wherever it appears rather than at a line start (a program sharing the descriptor can take the line start away, but not the token). It is the **last** thing sideeye writes, on every path -- the digest is recorded when the report lands and emitted at the exit, after the text report, so a reader that takes the first line of sideeye's output sees what it always saw — through a pipe or a file, where the verdict word is never coloured.
- The declared checker's output in each explored world is **also** captured to `<work>/checker-output.txt`, so the evidence bundle can quote the exhibit's last line. On your terminal each line is re-emitted with the world it came from — `world 3: ` for crash point 3, the number the report's `crash point 3 of n` carries, and `baseline: ` for the un-killed world — beside the falsification gate's `falsify: ` lines, the starting-state probe's `start: ` lines when it refuses (#756), and a recovery's `recovery world 3: ` and `recovery world 3 check: ` (its controls are `recovery falsify: `, `recovery baseline: ` and `recovery baseline check: `). The checker's stderr is captured into the same file in the order it was written and comes out on Sideeye's standard output with the same mark, not on Sideeye's standard error (#707). Empty lines are skipped, a line too long for the report's 32 KiB output buffer is dropped with a note on Sideeye's standard error, and a capture over 1 MiB is not re-emitted at all; the file keeps the checker's bytes unmarked, and holds whichever world ran last, which is the un-killed baseline. A capture that cannot be opened does not stop the run: the checker runs uncaptured, its standard output and standard error reach Sideeye's own directly and unmarked, the verdict rests on its exit status as before, and the bundle reports its diagnostic as unreadable.
- `--fresh-state` (replay only) empties and recreates the case's state directory before setup, for a caller that cannot hand over a pristine one — a second replay in the same directory would otherwise die in the leftovers of the first.
- `--leave-crash-state` (replay only) ends the run with the state directory rewritten to what the kill left at the case's crash point, before the checker ran — names, kinds and contents, and permission bits (a directory with its owner's bits added; not set-id or sticky bits, and not the state directory's own mode) — so it can be read as the crash left it instead of rebuilt by hand from the evidence table. It is written after any `--recovery` and whatever the verdict: a replay whose FAIL did not reproduce still leaves the crash state, and the report's `crash state` line and `crash_state_left` say whether it was left and, when not, why — a run that stopped before a verdict leaves none, and a rewrite that fails leaves a FAIL a FAIL. Timestamps and ownership are the rewrite's, two names of one file come back as two files, a directory the engine cannot read comes back empty, and an absolute symlink still points where it did. A process the replay could not contain (a `setsid` child on macOS) that writes after the rewrite changes it silently. `--json` inside the state directory, or in a directory that does not exist yet, is refused with it. Not offered through the MCP server.
- One run at a time in a work directory: a run locks `<work>/run.lock` before `--fresh-state` empties anything and before its setup, and holds it until it exits; a run that names a work directory another run holds is refused as a SETUP ERROR naming that run's pid, before it writes anything there or empties a state (#816). Two runs in one work directory would read each other's traces and reports; give each its own `--work`. `run.lock` has to be a regular file with one link — yours, unless the run just made it — since the run writes its pid into it; anything else there is refused. On a filesystem without locks the lock is skipped and nothing is refused.
- A state directory with anything mounted inside it — a bind mount, a container volume, a disk image — is refused naming the mount point, before anything mounted there is removed: a SETUP ERROR when it is there before the recording run, an UNKNOWN when one appears later. Every world empties and rebuilds the state directory, and what is mounted inside it belongs to another tree (#817). On Linux the mount table (`/proc/self/mountinfo`) is read for this, and a host where it cannot be read is refused the same way; on both Linux and macOS the state is also walked for a directory on another device. A mount point that is the state directory itself is fine; a btrfs subvolume inside it is refused like a mount, because its device differs.
- Exit codes: **0 PASS, 1 FAIL, 2 UNKNOWN, 3 SETUP ERROR** — and UNKNOWN is never 0.
- When standard output is a terminal, `NO_COLOR` is unset or empty and `TERM` is not `dumb`, the text report's verdict word — PASS, FAIL, UNKNOWN, SETUP ERROR — is coloured; otherwise Sideeye adds no escape sequence of its own. Only standard output is asked, so `sideeye explore … > report.txt` typed at a terminal writes no colour to the file; a CI runner that gives its steps a terminal (Buildkite, `docker run -t`) colours the word, and `NO_COLOR=1` turns it off there. There is no flag to force colour (#712).
- `sideeye completions zsh|bash|fish` prints a completion script for that shell: it offers exactly the subcommands; after a subcommand, its positional argument where its usage line has one (a case file, a command name, a shell) and then exactly the flags its usage lines list — explore's and preflight's two lines together, so after `--config` the script still offers `--state`, which the run then refuses — with a value-taking flag's value completed as a file where the usage names a path, as its listed words where it lists them, and not at all otherwise. The script is built from the usage lines `sideeye help` prints, so it offers the flags this binary's help lists. Load it: bash (3.2 and later) `eval "$(sideeye completions bash)"` in `~/.bashrc`; zsh, after `compinit`, `eval "$(sideeye completions zsh)"` in `~/.zshrc`, or the output saved as `_sideeye` in a directory on `$fpath`; fish `sideeye completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/sideeye.fish` (#712).
- Command strings split on spaces, no quoting. An argument that carries a space uses the argv form instead: `operation = ["mytool", "commit", "-m", "a message with spaces"]` — one line, passed verbatim.
- **A string-form command that looks written for a shell runs as written, with a warning** (#706, ADR 0095). Its quotes reach the program as characters, and a whole word a shell would act on — `&&`, `||`, `|`, `|&`, `&`, `;`, `(`, `)`, a redirection such as `>`, `2>&1` or `1>/dev/null`, a word beginning `$` or `~/`, a lone `~`, a backquote, a `$` a shell would expand (one followed by a name, `{` or `(`) anywhere in a word, quoted in double quotes or not, a leading `NAME=value` — reaches it as an argument, unexpanded. Where a setup, operation, check or recovery command (a toml value or a flag) holds a quote or such a word, Sideeye says so in one sentence naming the command and, for quotes, the argv form that groups what they meant (for a flag, as the line a sideeye.toml would take; a `[recovery]` command has no argv form, and neither has a word the argv form cannot spell — an empty one, one with a `"` or `\` — so those are pointed at a script). Where a shell would have expanded a `$` or a backquote, no argv is offered: it would carry the unexpanded text. A glob is not looked at, and passes as written either way. A toml command value with an inner `"` followed at once by `#` — `check = "grep -c "#include" f"` — is read as ending at that quote, with the rest a comment; it is accepted as it always was, and the warning says what the command became. The sentence is in the report as `warning`, in the JSON as `define_warnings`, in `sideeye mcp`'s summary, and on Sideeye's standard error as `sideeye: warning: …`, written once at the end so the first line of merged output is still the verdict — which also reaches a run that ends in a SETUP ERROR, and `preflight`. A replay is not looked at: its case holds commands an exploration already read. Left alone: a symbol inside a word (`x=n*10`, `ggiX<esc>`, `~>1.6`, `%(title)s`), a version constraint (`>=1.6`), a glob, a brace, a backslash outside quotes (`a\ b`) — each means what it says to a program run without a shell. A toml value the parser refuses as not one double-quoted string — `state = './state'`, `expected_status = 0`, `operation = "tool "two words""` — is refused with the line it would have been read as, when that line parses back as one value the writer could have meant: a trailing comment is kept, a value that reads two ways (`"a" "b"`) and one holding bytes the report would have to rewrite get no line.
- A define spelled as argv lives in a toml; `preflight --config` reads it, as explore does.
- **A command, option or argument Sideeye does not accept is answered in one line that names what was typed and, when one is close, the nearest spelling that command accepts — never by the whole reference; `sideeye help <command>` (or `sideeye <command> --help`) prints that command's own synopsis and flags** (#705). A value is named as well as a flag (`--observe bogus` says `bogus`). The command's own help carries each flag's first sentence and every sentence of its entry that begins `Caution:`; `sideeye help` prints the whole reference, and `sideeye --version` is `sideeye version`. `sideeye <command> --help` is answered only as those three words: `explore --state X --help` and `explore --help --state X` are refused with that said, because the parser may already have acted on what came before it — `--json` removes the report at its path.

A FAIL saves its counterexample to `<work>/cases/NNNNNN.json`, writes an evidence bundle carrying the same id under `<work>/evidence/NNNNNN.json` — a directory of its own, so a reader of `cases/*.json` is never handed one, and prints the ready-to-paste `sideeye replay` line beside an `evidence` line carrying the command that renders the bundle, `sideeye evidence <bundle>`. `sideeye evidence <case.json>` renders that bundle as Markdown for a maintainer who has never used Sideeye — the paths whose before, completed and crashed states differ, whether each existed before the operation and whether its old bytes survive elsewhere inside the judged state, the two operations around the crash point, the checker's result and its last output line, the replay command and the run's own caveats. It runs nothing and produces no verdict: exit 0 when it renders, 3 when the bundle cannot be read. Every field is something the run measured or the word `unknown`, and nothing is ranked ([docs/evidence.md](evidence.md)). When some world failed your checker and it is not the overall earliest, that world is saved as its own case beside the first and the text report gains a `checker red` section naming it — two files, both replayable; one file when the two exhibits are the same world, and none of this when no world failed the checker. Replay re-runs the same pipeline restricted to that crash point; when the code changed underneath the case, it says `case no longer applies` instead of guessing. The path you hand it has to be an ordinary file: a pipe, a device or a process substitution is refused rather than read, because a case that cannot be read whole is not a case — and because reading one that never ends would leave the run with no exit code at all (#400). A relative `define.state` inside a case resolves **against the case file's own directory**, the way a relative path in a `sideeye.toml` resolves against the toml (ADR 0007) — so the same case names the same state directory from anywhere, and replay empties the directory the case meant rather than one named by whoever happened to invoke it. Cases this engine saves always store the resolved absolute path, so this rule is about the hand-written ones.

### The flags the define does not spell

Seven flags never appear in a `sideeye.toml`: they belong to the run rather than to the question.

- `--observe wrappers|syscalls|supervised` — where operations are counted. The default, `wrappers`, counts at the interposed libc entry points, with buffered stdio observed at flush granularity. `syscalls` (Linux) counts at the kernel boundary instead, through a seccomp filter and a `SIGSYS` handler inside the target's own process — the only way to see an operation libc issues from *inside* itself (an `fwrite` past the buffer), or one that never reaches libc at all: a raw `syscall(SYS_write, ...)`, or a runtime like Go's that issues every file call directly. Its trap set is every operation that can be a crash point. Check the second entry of the README's constraint list before reaching for it: under this mode an `exec`'d image the shim cannot be loaded into dies at its first state-changing call, which is the one limit that changes what the target does instead of making Sideeye refuse. `supervised` (Linux 5.19 or later, aarch64 and x86_64; #217, ADR 0089) counts the same operations from **outside** the target: the engine starts the operation through `sideeye __filter-exec`, which installs a seccomp user-notification filter and execs it, and no shim is loaded. **A statically linked target, which the other two modes refuse as `no_shim_marker`, is counted and reaches a verdict under this mode**, with the oracle watching the same run (one that starts a dynamic child, which those modes let past their gate because the child carries the shim, is sent here by three refusals in the shapes measured to be crossed, [report-schema](report-schema.md), #685; its other refusals keep their steps); where it cannot be judged it refuses with an existing reason. Each state-changing call waits for the engine, which counts it and lets it run, or at the crash point kills the run while the call is still waiting, so the call never runs. It needs a cgroup v2 the engine can create cgroups in (a setup error names it otherwise). Its walls: a run whose writes come from two or more threads refuses `multiple_threads_detected`, because the thread-order records are the shim's — and recording thread creations and exits from outside instead is not built: of 50 recording runs this mode refused for jj, OpenTofu, codex and doctl, 48 hold a hand-over between writing threads that neither a thread's creation nor its exit orders, and doctl's other two were ordered by a creation the Go scheduler happened to make (#687, `spike/dogfood/2026-10-10-thread-order/`; tombi, refused in 1 of 36 supervised explores and 3 of 20 replays while its preflight was accepted 26 times of 26, was not read); a target that installs its own seccomp filter can return an error or trap for a call before this one sees it; `no_new_privs` is set, so a setuid child does not gain its privilege; i386-compat and x32 calls are not seen. Reading a call's paths needs the engine to read the target's memory, which Yama's `ptrace_scope` governs: at 2 or 3 every in-scope operation is unplaceable and the run refuses rather than guesses. The filter outlives the engine only as long as the engine does: were the engine to die mid-run, the target's next watched call would fail with `ENOSYS` — a changed target, which the run that follows cannot report because nobody is left to report it. On a run that reached the oracle comparison — whether it agreed or refused — and under `--allow-unverified`, the report's `oracle` line says who counted: the supervising engine, from outside the target, with no shim loaded. A run refused before the comparison (a thread refusal, say) says `not compared`, as in every mode. **A case saved under `--observe syscalls` or `--observe supervised` records the mode, and is replayed under it with no `--observe` given** — by `sideeye replay <case>` and by `sideeye_replay_case` over MCP alike (#691, ADR 0100). The report's `replay` line still names the mode, which a replay accepts when it matches; an `--observe` naming another mode is refused by name, because the case's crash point is a number in its own mode's count. Such a case is `case_version` 6, which a binary before this change refuses as unparseable rather than replays; a case counted under the default keeps the version its define asks for. A case saved before this change records nothing, and is replayed under the flag, or the default, as it always was.
- `--oracle <strace>` — the Linux oracle: the recording run is wrapped in strace and the shim's account is compared against strace's. **Refused on macOS** as `platform_unsupported`, whatever the path names (macOS has no strace, and the engine reads strace's account and nothing else); the refusal names `--oracle-fs-usage` and `--allow-unverified` under explore and replay, and says to drop the flag under preflight, which takes neither (#702).
- `--oracle-fs-usage` — the macOS oracle, in place of `--oracle`. It compares the recording run against `fs_usage`, which needs root, so `sudo` must already hold credentials (`sudo -v` first, in the same terminal — the cache is per-terminal); the run refuses rather than prompting. It is narrower than strace. `fs_usage` prints only a rename's old path and cuts long pathnames from the left (both measured), so a rename it cannot match and a state directory deep enough to be cut are refusals rather than agreements. It cannot account for other processes, so a child the shim saw, or the subject replacing its own image, is UNKNOWN under it. A single-process run with neither, whose state-directory writes come from one thread the shim recorded — the main thread or a worker — is explored and judged under it as under `--oracle` (ADR 0060), however `--work` is spelled — through a symlink such as the default `/tmp/sideeye-work`, or relative — and whether the target writes through `/tmp`, `/var` (where `$TMPDIR` lies) or `/etc` (#795, ADR 0128), and so is one that writes its standard output and standard error, or moves a file onto a standard descriptor with `dup` or `dup2` and writes through it, as GNU `dd of=` does (#796, ADR 0122): the engine tells the reader where descriptors 0, 1 and 2 point — 0 and 1 it set up, 2 is its own stderr — since the capture cannot, and `fs_usage` runs without a class filter, which is what prints `dup` and `dup2` with both numbers. A descriptor the reader cannot place still refuses: a pipe the target makes itself, or a `socketpair` it writes before any socket call names it, for which `fs_usage` prints no number, or a number moved from one the capture never saw opened. A run in which `fs_usage` reports a buffer overrun on its stderr, or whose stderr cannot be read back, refuses, since a dropped event is an operation neither account holds.
- `--allow-unverified` — accept a PASS with no completeness check. On macOS this is the answer when no privilege is available: SIP leaves DTrace's syscall provider with no probes even as root, and the one candidate that measured oracle-shaped, `fs_usage`, requires it. The report says which claim was made, and this one is weaker.
- `--world-timeout <s>` — a wall-clock budget per explored world (1 to 86400, off by default). A world's operation still running when the budget expires is sent `SIGKILL` and refused UNKNOWN `child_timed_out`, with the budget in the message. Worlds only: a recording run, a setup command or a checker that hangs still hangs, so this is not a promise of a hang-free run. Setting it also resets `SIGCHLD` to its default disposition for the whole run, and it is not settable over MCP today.
- `--stop-when-orphaned` — stop at the next world boundary if the process that launched the run exits (UNKNOWN, `parent_exited`). The MCP server passes it on every explore and replay: agent hosts restart MCP servers routinely, and an orphaned exploration otherwise keeps killing processes and rewriting its state directory with nobody left to report to. A run that hangs before a boundary is out of reach, unless the server itself is stopped by a signal it can catch: it hands that signal to the engine (next item).
- **Stopped by a signal, a run stops what it is running first** (#819, ADR 0124). `sideeye explore`, `replay` and `preflight` — `demo` runs one of them — and `sideeye mcp`, stopped by SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGPIPE (Ctrl-C, a cancelled CI job, a closed terminal), stop the child they are waiting on — a setup, the operation and strace with it, a checker, a recovery — the way a world over `--world-timeout` is stopped: `SIGKILL` to its process group, and everything in the cgroup the engine made for it where it made one; `fs_usage` is stopped as at the end of a recording. The MCP server hands the signal to the engine it is waiting on, which does the same. Then the process ends by the signal it received, with a line on stderr naming it; a run stopped before its verdict writes no report and prints no `json sha256=` line. When the child it waits on is one that signal cannot end — in an uninterruptible wait, or under credentials it switched to — that child's group is named on the line after 5 seconds (20 for the engine `sideeye mcp` waits on, which has its own child and `fs_usage` to stop first) and left running; a second signal ends the run at once, with `fs_usage` sent the SIGINT that stops it but not waited for. What it does not do: a process that left the child's group is stopped only where there is a cgroup, and one further down that the signal cannot reach — under sudo, say — survives unnamed, both as under `--world-timeout`; a signal ignored when Sideeye started (`nohup`) stays ignored, and the children it starts inherit that; the state directory holds what the stopped child left, not the state from before the run; and SIGKILL, which no process can catch, still leaves the run's children running.
- `--state-under <dir>` (explore, replay and preflight) — the directory the state must resolve strictly inside; anything else is refused before setup runs. A case file names its own state directory, and a config its own, and all three commands empty and rebuild it — explore and replay before the recording run and every world, preflight before its run or each of `--twice`'s two — so this is how a caller that vetted only the file's path bounds where it may point the deletion. The MCP server passes its `SIDEEYE_MCP_STATE_ROOT` (default: the server root) on every exploration (#765), every replay and every preflight (#717, #815).

## Example

Real output — the same planted delete-before-rename bug the demo uses (`spike/toys/toy.c`), explored with a checker and the strace oracle; the paths are the container's, and the engine hands the target its state directory via `SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR` and, for the toy, `TOY_STATE`:

```
$ TOY=/tmp/se/toy-bug /work/zig-out/bin/sideeye explore --state /tmp/se/state \
    --setup "/tmp/se/toy-bug init" --operation "/tmp/se/toy-bug rotate" \
    --check /work/spike/check.sh --shim /work/zig-out/lib/libsideeye_shim.so \
    --work /tmp/se/work --oracle /usr/bin/strace

falsify: doctor says 'healthy' but the key is unloadable
world 5: doctor says 'healthy' but the key is unloadable
FAIL  1 of 6 explored worlds violated an invariant

invariant   built-in atomicity, and the checker
earliest    crash point 5 of 5
            after  unlink(/tmp/se/state/key.json)
            before rename(/tmp/se/state/key.json.tmp)
path        key.json
observed    present before and after the operation, but gone from the crashed state
cwd         /work  (none declared: Sideeye's own)

explored    6 worlds (crash points 5 + 1 baseline)
expected    exit 0
atomicity   1 path(s) judged pre-or-post
oracle      agreed on 5 operations (88 syscall lines examined, 12 in scope of the judged state), witness strace
metadata    none observed. Restore reproduces permission bits (read, write and execute; a directory's owner bits are added) but not ownership, set-id or sticky bits, or timestamps: crash worlds start from the recorded permission bits, with timestamps assigned during restore
checker     falsified before the run (corrupted state -> check failed); ran in 6 world(s)
l1          no marker configured
case        /tmp/se/work/cases/000001.json
replay      sideeye replay /tmp/se/work/cases/000001.json --shim /work/zig-out/lib/libsideeye_shim.so
evidence    sideeye evidence /tmp/se/work/evidence/000001.json
processes   single process
not tested  power loss, torn writes, concurrent processes

reproduce   (cd /work && unset SIDEEYE_KILL_GROUP && : > /tmp/se/work/trace-repro.bin && SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR=/tmp/se/state SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR_ALT= SIDEEYE_TRACE_PATH=/tmp/se/work/trace-repro.bin LD_PRELOAD=/work/zig-out/lib/libsideeye_shim.so SIDEEYE_KILL_AT=5 SIDEEYE_SEQ_BASE= SIDEEYE_OBSERVE=wrappers SIDEEYE_RUN_CGROUP= SIDEEYE_KILL_CGROUP= SIDEEYE_KILL_ASIDE= /tmp/se/toy-bug rotate </dev/null)
```

Read the account block, not just the verdict: `explored` says how much was looked at, `oracle` says a second witness (strace) checked the shim's account against the kernel's, `checker` says the invariant was proven able to fail before the run began, `cwd` says where the define's commands ran — Sideeye's own directory here, because this define declared none — and `not tested` names what this verdict is silent about. A PASS and an UNKNOWN print the lines they share with this block under the same keys, in the same columns and the same order — `cwd`, `apparatus`, `warning` and `recovery` first, then a blank line, then the rest — and each verdict prints a fixed set: a PASS has no `replay` or `evidence`, which belong to a counterexample, and an UNKNOWN leaves out `explored`, `oracle`, `metadata` and `checker`, because a refusal can be raised before the exploration and would print figures for crash points it never reached (the JSON report carries all of them on every verdict). On an explore's FAIL that saved its case, `replay`, `evidence` and `reproduce` are commands that run as printed (#709, #711). `replay` and `evidence` run with `sideeye` on `PATH` — `replay` from the directory the `cwd` line names when the define declared none, since an undeclared define's commands run where Sideeye is started, and with the `--observe` mode the run used, which a replay also takes from the case itself when the mode is not the default. `reproduce` runs in a POSIX shell once the define's setup has left the state it starts from — as often as it is pasted: in a subshell, it changes to the directory the commands ran in, empties its trace file (the shim numbers on from the highest number a trace already holds, so a second paste into a full one would never reach the crash point), sets the variables Sideeye hands a world — except that a pasted line runs in neither a world's process group nor its cgroup, so it unsets `SIDEEYE_KILL_GROUP`, whose mere presence would take the reader's own shell down with the target, and pins the cgroup ones empty; and it does not carry `TOY_STATE`, the demo toy's own name for the state directory, which the toy reads `SIDEEYE_STATE_DIR` for when it is unset — and runs the operation's own argv with standard input from `/dev/null`, as every command Sideeye runs has it. Its standard output is the terminal, where a world's was a file. **A `SIDEEYE_KILL_AT` or `SIDEEYE_KILL_GROUP` left exported in your shell no longer stops any run** (#822, ADR 0126): Sideeye removes both from its own environment when it starts, and only a world, armed by Sideeye at its own crash point, carries them; `SIDEEYE_MCP_CHILD_ENV` refuses to name either. The line starts from the state the setup left, not the rebuilt one the recording and every world start from (#815), so a target that reads what the rebuild changes — the order tmpfs, btrfs or XFS list a directory in, an owner, a timestamp — can meet another operation at that number; `replay` starts from the rebuilt state. It dies in front of the same crash point, in the process that reaches it: where the run admitted writing children, the rest of the tree keeps running, so the state can go further than the report's. Every value is quoted where a shell would read it otherwise, and a bare first word is quoted too, so an alias of that name in an interactive shell is not what runs. The line keeps the placeholder `<operation>`, with no `cd`, when the operation or its directory holds a byte the report defangs (rather than print the byte, or a defanged command that names something else), when Sideeye could not name the directory, or when the command would not fit the text report's output buffer. A replay's own FAIL prints the sentence it always did on `replay` and `-` on `evidence`; a FAIL whose case could not be written, `-` on both; under `--observe supervised`, `reproduce` names the replay line, the one command that reproduces a crash point counted from outside the target.

The `check` script is where your invariants live. This one cross-examines the tool's own diagnostic — a tool is allowed to be broken as long as it says so; the violation is the claim and the observable truth disagreeing:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
claim=$("$TOY" doctor 2>/dev/null) || claim="unhealthy"
"$TOY" load-key >/dev/null 2>&1 && reality="loadable" || reality="unloadable"

case "$claim:$reality" in
    healthy:loadable | unhealthy:unloadable) exit 0 ;;
    *) echo "doctor says '$claim' but the key is $reality" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
```

The full version is [`spike/check.sh`](../spike/check.sh). Sideeye refuses to trust a checker it has not seen fail: before exploring, it corrupts the state and requires the check to reject it. A checker that cannot fail makes the run UNKNOWN, not PASS. More worked checkers: [docs/checker-cookbook.md](checker-cookbook.md).

## What it is for after the first find

The finding is not the durable artifact — the declaration is. A `sideeye.toml` and its checker are the question, not the answer, so re-asking it after the tool changes is `explore --config` again, and the report says what it looked at that time rather than assuming the last run still holds. A saved case is deliberately narrower: it names one crash point in one recording, and when the recording moves underneath it the answer is `case no longer applies` rather than a silent pass — which is what makes a case worth keeping in CI. This repository keeps its own oldest finding that way, re-recorded under the current trace contract on every push to main and every pull request (the `timew-regression` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`). And because a target Sideeye cannot fully observe is UNKNOWN and never exit 0, a machine caller can tell *checked and clean* from *not checked*, which is the distinction an unattended run has to get right. What none of that does is constrain what your declared operation may do — that boundary is the config you vet, as [the MCP page](mcp.md) says.
